title: Load Balancer
description: Learn why a single server collapses under heavy traffic spikes, and how reverse-proxy load balancers distribute load across server clusters using algorithms like Round Robin.
learningObjectives: Identify the single point of failure and bottleneck in single-server architecture
Understand horizontal scaling vs vertical scaling
Deploy a Load Balancer to dynamically distribute 1,000 concurrent user requests
Observe CPU drop from 95% down to 40% and latency drop from 3,000ms to 300ms

steps.title: Analyze Initial Failure
steps.description: Notice how all 1,000 users are hitting Server 1 directly. The single CPU is redlining at 95% and response times are 3.0 seconds!

steps.title: Add Load Balancer
steps.description: Place an Nginx/ALB reverse-proxy between incoming clients and your backend instances.

steps.title: Scale to Multi-Server Fleet
steps.description: Spawn Server 2 and Server 3. Watch traffic distribute evenly across all nodes.

challenge.title: Your Website Crashed!
challenge.scenario: A sudden viral post drove 50,000 visitors to your e-commerce site. The single host server CPU shot to 100% and connection timeouts spiked.
challenge.question: What core component should be added first to distribute the incoming traffic across multiple web servers?
hints: Hint 1: Traffic is unevenly distributed across your single compute instance.
Hint 2: Adding multiple application servers can share the load horizontally.
Hint 3: Think about a reverse-proxy Load Balancer using Round Robin to balance network sockets.

options.label: In-Memory Cache (Redis)
options.explanation: While Redis caches data, it doesn't distribute incoming HTTP socket connections to multiple backend compute instances.

options.label: Load Balancer (Reverse Proxy)
options.explanation: Correct ✅ Traffic overload was caused by a single server bottleneck. A Load Balancer distributes incoming network requests across a pool of healthy backend servers.

options.label: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
options.explanation: CDNs cache static edge assets like images and CSS, but dynamic API traffic and authentication still need backend compute distribution.

title: Cache
description: When 10,000 users request the exact same product catalog data, hitting the relational database 10,000 times will melt your disk I/O. Add a high-speed Redis cache.
learningObjectives: Understand the Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) architecture pattern
Compare disk I/O (15ms - 500ms) with RAM memory lookups (<1ms)
Reduce 10,000 direct database hits down to just 100 cache misses
Achieve 99% cache hit ratio and drop latency from 1,200ms to 15ms

steps.title: Identify Database Bottleneck
steps.description: 10,000 users are querying the exact same trending item. Every single query locks rows in PostgreSQL, causing DB disk saturation.

steps.title: Deploy In-Memory Redis Cluster
steps.description: Insert an ultra-fast Redis cache between the application layer and PostgreSQL.

challenge.title: Database Disk I/O Saturation
challenge.scenario: A flash sale on a popular gaming console has 10,000 concurrent shoppers repeatedly loading the exact same product details page. PostgreSQL CPU is at 99%.
challenge.question: What is the most effective architectural solution to shield the database from identical repeated read queries?
hints: Hint 1: Upgrading hardware (vertical scaling) becomes exponentially expensive and hits physical limits.
Hint 2: Thousands of users are querying the exact same static or semi-static product information.
Hint 3: Serving repeated data from in-memory RAM (e.g., Redis Cache) bypasses expensive disk I/O.

options.label: Upgrade Database to 128 vCPUs (Vertical Scaling)
options.explanation: Vertical scaling is prohibitively expensive and quickly hits physical hardware limits without addressing the root inefficiency.

options.label: Add In-Memory Cache (Redis / Memcached)
options.explanation: Correct ✅ By serving popular items directly from ultra-fast RAM, database hits drop from 10,000 to ~100 (a 99% reduction), reducing latency to mere milliseconds.

options.label: Spin up a second independent database with copy of data
options.explanation: Unsynchronized independent databases cause severe data inconsistency and split-brain states without replication logic.

title: Database Scaling
description: When platform traffic surges 10x, write locks and complex reporting queries overwhelm a single primary database. Distribute read queries across multiple Read Replicas.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between Read-Heavy vs Write-Heavy access patterns
Distribute 90% read traffic across replica pools using asynchronous replication
Protect primary transactional integrity under 10x traffic surges

steps.title: 10x Traffic Spike Overwhelms DB
steps.description: Analytics, user profiles, and feed requests are competing with order checkouts on a single Postgres master.

steps.title: Configure Read Replicas
steps.description: Spawn two asynchronous read replicas. Route all SELECT queries to replicas, reserving the primary strictly for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

challenge.title: The 95/5 Read-Write Ratio
challenge.scenario: Your social network has 95% read traffic (feed scrolling, viewing profiles) and only 5% write traffic (posting updates). The single database is struggling to process reads.
challenge.question: Which architecture pattern best scales this read-dominant workload horizontally?
hints: Hint 1: Note that 95% of queries are reads (SELECT) and only 5% are writes (INSERT/UPDATE).
Hint 2: Complex sharding is overkill when writes are already very low.
Hint 3: Setting up Read Replicas allows you to route all SELECT queries across replicas while keeping writes on the primary.

options.label: Complex Range Sharding across 20 shards
options.explanation: Sharding adds immense operational complexity, cross-shard join headaches, and rebalancing overhead before simpler read replication is exhausted.

options.label: Primary Database with Read Replicas
options.explanation: Correct ✅ In read-heavy systems (95% reads), adding read replicas allows horizontal read scaling while keeping writes consolidated on the primary node.

options.label: Cache all user data inside browser localStorage
options.explanation: Client localStorage is limited to ~5MB, vulnerable to tampering, and cannot reflect dynamic multi-user updates.
